concepts.title: REST vs. gRPC: Choosing an API Style
concepts.description: REST and gRPC aren't two syntaxes for the same idea. They make different bets about who's calling, how often, and what a contract violation should cost, and picking the wrong one for a given caller is a recurring, expensive mistake.
learningObjectives: Describe REST's contract (resources, HTTP verbs, JSON-over-HTTP) and gRPC's contract (protobuf schemas, HTTP/2, generated stubs).
Explain concretely what gRPC buys over REST (binary payloads, strict schemas, native streaming, codegen) and what it costs (browser support, human-readability, tooling maturity).
Explain why REST's loose schema is an advantage for public APIs and a liability for high-volume internal calls.
Given a caller description (public third-party, internal high-throughput service, real-time stream), recommend REST or gRPC and justify it.
Identify the common mistake of picking a protocol based on performance benchmarks alone, ignoring who actually has to call the API.

sections.heading: Two Different Contracts for Talking Between Services
sections.body:
**REST** describes an API as a set of *resources* (`/orders/42`, `/users/7/orders`) manipulated with standard HTTP verbs (`GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`), with a body, almost always JSON, carrying the data. The protocol itself mandates no schema format; the shape of the JSON is whatever the API author documents, often informally, or formalizes afterward with a tool like OpenAPI. Any HTTP client can call a REST API (a browser, `curl`, a mobile app, another service) because HTTP and JSON are close to universal.

**gRPC** describes an API as a set of typed *procedures* defined up front in a `.proto` file, such as `GetOrder(OrderRequest) returns (OrderResponse)`, with every field's type and number declared. That file is compiled into client and server code (stubs) in whichever languages you need, so calling a remote gRPC method looks from the caller's side almost like calling a local function. Underneath, gRPC runs over HTTP/2 and serializes messages with Protocol Buffers (protobuf), a compact binary format, instead of human-readable JSON.

The deeper difference is where the contract lives and how strictly it's enforced. REST's contract is a convention you agree to and can drift from without anyone noticing; gRPC's contract is a schema the compiler enforces on both ends before a byte is sent.

sections.heading: Why REST Won by Default, and What It Costs
sections.body:
REST's dominance for public-facing and browser-facing APIs has good reasons behind it. Every browser, every language, and every debugging tool already speaks HTTP and JSON, so you can poke a REST API with `curl` or a browser address bar and read the response with no special tooling. That lowers the bar for third-party developers integrating with you, and it makes production debugging ("what did the client send?") trivial compared to inspecting a binary payload.

The cost shows up at volume and as the API changes. JSON is verbose: field names are repeated in every message instead of described once in a schema, so serialization time and payload size are worse than a binary format for the same data. That matters at millions of internal calls per second, much less at thousands of public ones per day. And because REST's "schema" is usually documentation (OpenAPI specs are optional and easy to let drift from the implementation), nothing stops a service from changing a field's type or removing a field without callers finding out until something breaks at runtime. REST also has no native long-lived, bidirectional stream: server-to-client push has to be added with polling, long-polling, Server-Sent Events, or WebSockets, and none of those is "REST" in the resources-and-verbs sense.

sections.heading: Why gRPC Exists and What It Buys You
sections.body:
gRPC targets the pain points that appear once many internal services call each other at high volume. Protobuf's binary encoding is smaller on the wire and faster to serialize and parse than JSON, because field names aren't repeated in each message: they're numbered once in the shared `.proto` schema and both sides know the mapping. HTTP/2 underneath multiplexes many concurrent requests over a single connection, avoiding the cost of opening a new connection (or exhausting a pool) per call, which matters when one service makes thousands of calls per second to another.

The schema is the other half of the pitch. Because the `.proto` file is compiled into typed client and server code, a caller can't construct a request with a wrong field type: the code won't compile. The compatibility rules are specific, too. Adding a field with a new number is safe for old readers, while changing a field's type or reusing a retired field number breaks them, and the `.proto` review is where that gets checked. Evolving the contract (adding a field, deprecating another) follows a checked process instead of an informal agreement that both sides hope stays in sync. gRPC also supports streaming natively: server-streaming (one request, a stream of responses), client-streaming, and bidirectional streaming are part of the protocol, not layered on afterward.

The costs are real, though. A gRPC service isn't callable from a browser without an extra translation layer (grpc-web plus a proxy, or a REST-to-gRPC gateway, the kind of job an API gateway is often given; the next lesson covers it). Debugging a live call means reaching for specialized tools, since the payload is binary. And every consumer needs the `.proto` file and a codegen step in their build, a tax on a third-party integrator who just wants to send an HTTP request from whatever language they have open.

sections.heading: Choosing Between Them: the Caller and the Traffic Shape
sections.body:
What matters is who is calling this API and how, not which one benchmarks faster in isolation. gRPC will usually win a raw throughput benchmark, and that is frequently irrelevant. A public API used by third-party developers, many with limited engineering time and no interest in running a protobuf toolchain, should almost always be REST (or REST/JSON alongside a GraphQL layer), because ubiquity and easy debugging matter more than shaving milliseconds off a call that happens a few times a second per customer. An internal mesh where fifteen microservices exchange tens of thousands of calls per second, written in a mix of Go, Java, and Python, is gRPC's target case: the throughput and schema-safety gains compound at that volume, and every caller is a team that controls its own build tooling and can absorb the codegen step. A feature where the server keeps pushing updates to the client (live order status, a real-time dashboard) leans toward gRPC's native streaming, or an alternative such as WebSockets, over simulating push with repeated polling.

A very common architecture uses both: a REST (or REST-plus-GraphQL) edge facing the public internet and browsers, in front of an internal fleet of services that talk to each other over gRPC, with an API gateway translating between the two. Neither protocol is legacy or modern in an absolute sense; they're specialized for different callers.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake: Choosing by Benchmark Instead of by Caller
sections.body: The recurring, expensive mistake is picking gRPC for a public-facing API because "it's faster," then finding that a meaningful fraction of prospective integrators can't or won't adopt it. Some can't call it from a browser without extra infrastructure; some don't want a protobuf toolchain in their build for an integration they expected to be a five-minute `curl` command. The inverse mistake also happens: keeping a chatty JSON-over-HTTP REST API between two internal services that call each other tens of thousands of times a second, paying measurable latency and CPU on serialization that a schema-checked binary protocol would avoid, out of habit or unfamiliarity with gRPC. In both cases the fix isn't a universal rule ("always gRPC" or "always REST"). Ask who is on the other end of this call, and match the protocol to the answer.

examples.title: The Same Operation, REST vs. gRPC
examples.explanation: The REST version is readable with nothing but a browser or `curl`: you can see what was sent and received, and any HTTP client in any language can build that JSON body by hand. The gRPC version needs the `.proto` file and a codegen step before `order_client.ShipOrder(...)` can be written, but once that exists the caller gets compile-time checking that `order_id` is an integer and `carrier` is a string, which the REST version can't enforce beyond hoping the caller read the documentation. Neither payload shown reflects gRPC's wire format, which is protobuf's binary encoding, smaller and faster to parse than the JSON; the gRPC side is written as pseudocode for readability.

examples.title: Native Streaming: Order Status Updates
examples.explanation: gRPC's `stream` keyword makes server-to-client push part of the contract: one call is opened, and the server writes multiple responses onto it as the order's status changes, with no polling interval to guess and no wasted round trips when nothing changed. The REST version has no equivalent primitive. Polling is the closest fit, and it forces a tradeoff between wasted requests (poll too often) and staleness (poll too rarely) that the gRPC version never has to make. A REST API that needs push usually reaches for WebSockets or Server-Sent Events, which departs from REST's resources-and-verbs model instead of extending it.

examples.title: Schema Drift: What REST Doesn't Catch That gRPC Does
examples.explanation: This is the practical payoff of gRPC's stricter contract. The schema is the source both client and server code are generated from, so a breaking change has to happen in one reviewable place before it can reach production, instead of in whatever JSON-shaping code happens to run on the server. REST doesn't prevent this kind of drift. It relies on discipline (careful versioning, contract testing, deprecation policies) layered over a protocol that enforces nothing about field names or types. Teams running large REST APIs usually end up building that discipline by hand, with OpenAPI schemas checked in CI and consumer-driven contract tests, which re-derives with extra tooling some of what gRPC's compiled contract provides by default. Note that protobuf puts the field number on the wire, not the name, so renaming a field in a `.proto` file is wire-compatible; it's changing a field's type or reusing its number that breaks existing callers.

misconceptions.description: gRPC is strictly faster and more modern, so it should be preferred over REST whenever you have the choice.
misconceptions.clarification: gRPC usually wins on raw serialization speed and payload size, but "faster in a benchmark" isn't the deciding question for most APIs. Who has to call it is. A public API used by third-party developers benefits far more from REST's browser/curl/any-language accessibility and readable payloads than from gRPC's throughput advantage, which only matters at volumes most public integrators never approach. Preferring gRPC unconditionally trades away debuggability and ease of integration for a performance gain that is often irrelevant to the bottleneck.

misconceptions.description: The difference between REST and gRPC is basically just JSON vs. binary encoding -- a serialization format choice.
misconceptions.clarification: Serialization format is one visible difference, but the deeper one is where the contract lives and how strictly it's enforced. REST's shape is an informal convention (formalized only if you add OpenAPI and keep it in sync), while gRPC's `.proto` schema is compiled into both client and server code, so a type mismatch is a compile error instead of a runtime surprise. gRPC also supports bidirectional and server streaming as part of the protocol, and runs over HTTP/2's multiplexed connections. None of that is about JSON vs. binary.

exercises.prompt: A company is building two things at once: (1) a public weather API that thousands of third-party developers, many hobbyists with minimal tooling, will integrate with from browsers and simple scripts; (2) an internal fleet of 20 microservices exchanging roughly 50,000 calls per second among themselves, all written and deployed by the company's own engineering teams. Predict which protocol fits each system better, and justify each choice using the constraints given (not a general preference).
exercises.code:
System 1: public weather API
  - thousands of third-party integrators, many with minimal engineering tooling
  - called directly from browsers and simple scripts
  - call volume per integrator: low (a few requests per minute, typically)

System 2: internal microservice fleet
  - 20 services, all owned by the same engineering org
  - ~50,000 calls/sec between services
  - every caller already has a modern build toolchain
hints: For System 1, think about who has to integrate and what tooling they can realistically be expected to have -- does 'called directly from a browser' rule anything out?
For System 2, think about what 50,000 calls/sec does to JSON serialization overhead compared to a binary format, and whether the callers can absorb a codegen step.
The right answer isn't 'gRPC is always better' or 'REST is always simpler' -- match each system's actual callers and traffic shape to the protocol's actual strengths.
exercises.expectedAnswer: System 1 (public weather API) should be REST/JSON: third-party integrators, especially hobbyists, need to call the API with a browser, curl, or a simple script in whatever language they have, with no protobuf toolchain or generated stubs, and call volume per integrator is low enough that JSON's verbosity and REST's lack of a strict schema don't matter. System 2 (internal fleet) should be gRPC: all callers are internal teams with modern build tooling who can absorb a codegen step, 50,000 calls/sec is high enough that protobuf's smaller, faster-to-parse payloads and HTTP/2 multiplexing make a measurable difference, and the compiled .proto contracts prevent the schema drift that gets costlier to discover at runtime as the number of services grows.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The two systems differ on the two axes that should drive this decision: who is calling, and how much. System 1's callers are external, numerous, tooling-constrained, and individually low-volume. REST's universal accessibility (any HTTP client, readable payloads, no codegen) serves them, and gRPC's performance advantage would cost every integrator onboarding friction for a throughput benefit none of them needs. System 2's callers are internal, few, tooling-capable, and collectively very high-volume. gRPC's binary serialization and HTTP/2 multiplexing save measurable latency and CPU at 50,000 calls/sec, which JSON over HTTP/1.1 would pay for, and every caller can run a codegen step, so that cost is negligible. Picking gRPC for System 1 or REST for System 2 would sound defensible and be wrong, because each ignores the caller population in favor of a generic "which protocol is better" framing.

exercises.prompt: A team builds their entire public product API, including calls made from their own web app's browser JavaScript, as gRPC services, reasoning "gRPC is faster and more strictly typed than REST, so it's the better choice everywhere." Their web app cannot call the API at all without an extra piece of infrastructure they didn't plan for. Diagnose the mistake and describe the fix.
exercises.code:
Architecture as built:
  [Browser JavaScript] --???--> [gRPC service (order-service.proto)]
  -- browsers cannot open raw gRPC connections: gRPC relies on HTTP/2
     features (trailers, specific framing) that browser fetch/XHR APIs
     do not expose in the way a native gRPC client library expects
  -- the web app's own frontend, part of the SAME product, cannot
     directly call its own backend API
hints: gRPC's wire format depends on HTTP/2 features that browsers' JavaScript networking APIs don't expose the same way a native gRPC client does. Can a browser open a raw gRPC connection at all?

The mistake wasn't gRPC being slower or less typed -- it's that 'faster and stricter' was treated as the only criterion, ignoring who the caller actually is (in this case, partly their OWN browser-based frontend).
Think back to how gRPC services are made reachable from a browser. What extra piece of infrastructure does that require?
exercises.solutionCode:
FIXED ARCHITECTURE (one of two common directions):

Option A -- add a translation layer:
  [Browser JavaScript] --HTTP/JSON--> [REST-to-gRPC gateway] --gRPC--> [order-service]
  -- the gateway (often the same API gateway fronting other backends,
     see the API Gateways concept) exposes a REST/JSON facade and
     translates each call into the equivalent gRPC call internally

Option B -- use grpc-web + an Envoy-style proxy:
  [Browser JS, grpc-web client] --grpc-web protocol--> [proxy] --gRPC--> [order-service]
  -- grpc-web is a browser-compatible variant that still requires a proxy
     to bridge to real gRPC on the backend side

Either way: browser-facing traffic needs a REST (or grpc-web) facade;
plain gRPC cannot be the browser's direct calling convention.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The root mistake is treating "gRPC is faster and more strictly typed" as a universal ranking instead of a tradeoff that depends on the caller. Here one of the callers is the team's own browser frontend, which can't speak native gRPC the way a backend service can, because browser networking APIs don't expose the HTTP/2 primitives gRPC needs. That isn't a performance problem to optimize away; it's a protocol mismatch that needs an architectural fix. The practical fix is a translation layer between the browser and the gRPC backend: either a REST-to-gRPC gateway (a natural job for an API gateway, which is already the front door) or a grpc-web-compatible proxy. The browser then talks a browser-compatible protocol while internal services keep gRPC for service-to-service calls. The broader lesson is the one from earlier in this lesson: choose by caller, not by benchmark, and check that every caller can speak the protocol.

assessments.prompt: A team is deciding on a protocol for a brand-new internal service that will be called by three other internal services, all owned by the same engineering org, at a combined rate of about 40,000 requests per second, with no plans to ever expose it outside the company. Which factor most strongly favors choosing gRPC over REST here?
options: The high internal call volume and fully internal, tooling-capable caller population make gRPC's binary serialization, HTTP/2 multiplexing, and compiled schema safety worth their codegen cost, with none of REST's browser-accessibility advantages being relevant here.
REST cannot technically support 40,000 requests per second under any circumstances.
gRPC eliminates the need for API versioning entirely, since the schema is compiled into the code.
gRPC APIs are automatically more secure than REST APIs by default.
assessments.explanation: This scenario is gRPC's sweet spot: every caller is internal, already has modern build tooling, and the combined volume is high enough that protobuf's smaller payloads and HTTP/2 multiplexing give a measurable benefit, while REST's main selling points (browser/curl accessibility for third parties) don't apply because there are no such callers. The “gRPC APIs are automatically more secure…” option is false: security comes from how an API is authenticated and authorized, not from the protocol. The “REST cannot technically support 40,000 requests per…” option is false: REST over HTTP can handle very high volumes; the issue is efficiency and schema safety, not a hard ceiling. The “gRPC eliminates the need for API versioning…” option is false: gRPC still needs careful schema evolution (adding fields carefully, deprecating instead of removing, managing field numbers). It reduces accidental drift but doesn't remove the need to think about versioning.

assessments.prompt: A junior engineer asks: "Why don't we just rewrite our whole public API in gRPC? Wouldn't that make everything faster and more reliable?" Explain what's right and wrong about this idea, and what the actual decision should hinge on.
assessments.modelAnswer: What's right: gRPC would make some things faster and more reliable in specific technical ways. Protobuf's binary encoding is smaller on the wire and cheaper to serialize and parse than JSON, HTTP/2 multiplexing avoids some of the connection overhead REST calls accumulate, and a compiled .proto schema catches type mismatches and some breaking changes at build time instead of as runtime errors for callers who trusted an informal contract. For internal services owned by one org and calling each other at high volume, that combination is why gRPC is a strong default. What's wrong is applying that reasoning to a public API without asking who calls it. A public API's callers are outside your control: third-party developers, often with limited tooling, sometimes calling from a browser, sometimes just wanting to poke the API with curl to understand it before writing any integration code. gRPC can't be called from a browser without a translation layer, requires every caller to run a codegen step against your .proto files before writing any integration code, and produces binary payloads that can't be read or debugged without specialized tooling. All of that raises the bar for adoption in exactly the population a public API is trying to make things easy for. Rewriting the public API in gRPC would likely make the internal implementation faster while making the API harder to adopt and debug for its audience, a net loss even though every claim about gRPC's speed and type safety is true. The decision should hinge on the caller population and traffic shape for that API: public, tooling-constrained, browser-reachable audiences point toward REST (possibly with gRPC behind an API gateway that translates), while internal, high-volume, tooling-capable audiences point toward gRPC. There is no single global answer for every API a company runs.

assessments.prompt: A backend developer renames a JSON field in a REST API response from `total` to `totalAmount` without bumping any version number. What is the most likely consequence, and why does gRPC's approach reduce this specific risk?
options: Nothing changes for existing callers, since JSON field renames are automatically handled by all HTTP clients.
gRPC would have the exact same silent-renaming risk, since both protocols use text-based field names.
REST prevents this specific issue automatically through built-in field versioning that ships with the HTTP specification.

Existing callers reading response["total"] get a runtime error (a missing/undefined field) whenever that code path next executes, discovered only at runtime -- whereas a breaking change to a .proto field requires editing a shared, reviewable schema file that both client and server code are generated from, giving a natural point to catch and block it before it ships.
assessments.explanation: A renamed REST field means every existing caller reading response["total"] gets a KeyError or undefined at runtime, discovered whenever that code path next executes. The same change in a .proto file means editing a shared schema that client and server code are generated from, which is a natural place to require review and a compatibility check before it ships. The “Nothing changes for existing callers, since JSON…” option is false: the rename breaks anyone reading the old name. The “gRPC would have the exact same silent-renaming…” option is wrong: the compiled schema is what catches this class of change before production. The “REST prevents this specific issue automatically through…” option invents a built-in HTTP versioning mechanism that doesn't exist.

assessments.prompt: A feature needs the server to keep pushing live order-status updates to a client as they happen, without the client needing to guess a polling interval. Why does this favor gRPC over plain REST?
options: gRPC eliminates the need for the client to open any network connection at all.
gRPC's `stream` keyword makes server-to-client push a first-class part of the contract.
REST cannot be used over HTTP/2 under any circumstances, so it structurally cannot support any form of real-time updates.
REST is exclusively for reading data and gRPC is exclusively for writing data, so any 'live update' feature must use gRPC.
assessments.explanation: gRPC's `stream` keyword makes server-to-client push part of the contract, with no polling interval to guess, while REST's polling alternative forces a tradeoff between wasted requests (poll too often) and staleness (poll too rarely). The “REST cannot be used over HTTP/2 under…” option is false: REST APIs can run over HTTP/2; what they lack is a streaming primitive in the resources-and-verbs model. The “REST is exclusively for reading data…” option invents a read/write split that doesn't exist. The “gRPC eliminates the need for the client…” option is nonsense: gRPC calls still need a network connection; one connection just carries multiple pushed responses.

assessments.prompt: What goes wrong when a team picks gRPC for a public-facing API purely because benchmarks show it's faster?
options: The API automatically becomes less secure because gRPC does not support authentication of any kind.
Nothing goes wrong -- benchmark performance is described as the only factor that should ever matter when choosing a protocol.
A meaningful fraction of prospective integrators can't or won't adopt it.
gRPC services are described as being unable to run on cloud infrastructure at all, making public deployment impossible.
assessments.explanation: Choosing gRPC for a public API "because it's faster" leads to discovering that a meaningful fraction of prospective integrators can't or won't adopt it: some can't call it from a browser without extra infrastructure, and some don't want a protobuf toolchain in their build for an integration they expected to be a five-minute curl command. The “Nothing goes wrong -- benchmark performance…” option contradicts the point that caller population, not benchmark speed, should drive the decision. The “gRPC services are described as being unable…” option invents a cloud-deployment restriction. The “The API automatically becomes less secure…” option is false: gRPC supports authentication mechanisms.

concepts.title: Drawing Service Boundaries
concepts.description: Splitting a system into microservices is easy; splitting it along the right seams is the hard part. Get the boundary wrong and you get the coordination headaches of a monolith and the operational cost of distributed systems, with the benefits of neither.
learningObjectives: Explain why decomposing services by HTTP verb or by database table is a common, tempting, and usually wrong heuristic.
Define a service boundary in terms of business capability and data ownership rather than technical operations.
Identify concrete symptoms (chatty synchronous calls, shared tables, forced co-deployment) that indicate a boundary is drawn wrong.
Explain the 'distributed monolith' anti-pattern and why it combines the worst of both architectural worlds.
Recommend a practical, incremental process for discovering service boundaries rather than designing them all upfront.

sections.heading: The Tempting, Usually-Wrong Heuristics
sections.body:
Two heuristics for drawing service boundaries show up constantly because they feel objective and are easy to apply mechanically, and both are usually wrong. **"One service per verb"** decomposes by *operation*: a `create-order-service`, a `cancel-order-service`, a `ship-order-service`. It feels tidy because each service has a narrow, nameable job. But a business operation almost never maps to one verb. Cancelling an order needs to check its current status, adjust inventory, possibly issue a refund, and notify the customer, so "cancel an order" now means coordinating several services synchronously for what is conceptually one atomic action.

**"One service per table"** decomposes by *data*: a `users-service` owning the `users` table, an `orders-service` owning the `orders` table, mirroring the schema one-to-one. This also feels objective, since the boundary is wherever the schema already draws a line. But most queries and features need data from more than one table ("show a customer their order history with each item's current price"), so everyday operations end up reaching across a boundary that was drawn for schema tidiness and not for how the data is used together.

sections.heading: The Right Heuristic: Business Capability and Data Ownership
sections.body:
A service boundary works well when it wraps a **cohesive business capability**: a piece of the domain that changes for its own reasons, is owned end to end by one team, and encapsulates its own data so no other service reaches into its storage. "Order management" as a single service, owning order creation, cancellation, status, and the order table itself, is a better boundary than three verb-services, because the logic that changes together (a new cancellation rule, a new status transition) lives in one deployable unit instead of being spread across services that must be updated and redeployed in lockstep.

This lines up with an idea from domain-driven design called a **bounded context**: a boundary around a part of the domain where terms and rules mean one thing internally, even if a neighboring service uses a similar-sounding term differently. A `customer` in the billing service might carry different fields and invariants than a `customer` in support ticketing, and that's fine: they're different bounded contexts, not the same concept duplicated sloppily. Conway's Law matters here too. Service boundaries that don't roughly track team boundaries create constant cross-team coordination for changes that should be one team's decision, which is its own kind of wrong-boundary symptom, independent of the technical architecture.

sections.heading: Signals You've Drawn the Boundary Wrong
sections.body: A handful of observable symptoms reliably indicate a boundary problem, and they're worth watching for instead of debating boundaries in the abstract. **Chatty synchronous calls**: if handling one client request requires service A to call B synchronously, which calls C, which calls back into A, the "services" are probably one capability sliced along the wrong lines, and the network calls stand in for what should be in-process function calls. **Shared tables**: if two services read from or write to the same table (even with separate service code), the data ownership the boundary was supposed to establish doesn't exist, and a schema change can break a service that never knew it depended on it. **Forced co-deployment**: if changing service A routinely requires deploying a compatible change to service B at the same time, they aren't independent services operationally, however the code is organized. This symptom is common enough to have its own name, covered next. A fourth, organizational signal is that one team can't ship a change without another team's sign-off, which means the boundary and the team structure disagree.

sections.heading: The Distributed Monolith: Worst of Both Worlds
sections.body:
A system with several of those symptoms is usually called a **distributed monolith**. It has the operational overhead of microservices (network calls instead of function calls, independent deployments to coordinate, separate logging and monitoring to correlate, service discovery, retries and timeouts for calls that used to be reliable in-process) and still has the monolith's coupling, because the pieces can't change or deploy independently. It is worse than either a well-factored monolith or a well-factored set of microservices: you pay the complexity tax of distribution without the benefits (independent scaling, independent deployment, fault isolation) it is supposed to buy.

This usually happens for an understandable reason. Teams split a system into services *before* they understood where the seams in the domain were, often under pressure ("microservices are the modern architecture, so we should have several") and not in response to a scaling or team-structure problem the monolith was failing to solve.

sections.heading: A Practical, Incremental Process
sections.body:
The most reliable technique is to **start with a well-modularized monolith**: one deployable unit with clear internal module boundaries that already roughly track business capabilities. Split a module out into its own service only when there's a demonstrated reason: a scaling need for just that piece, a team that needs to deploy independently of everyone else, or a technology requirement (a different language or runtime) that the module needs. Splitting too early tends to reproduce the wrong-boundary symptoms above, because early guesses about where the seams are tend to be wrong, and moving a boundary after it has been baked into separate deployed services, separate databases, and separate on-call rotations is far more expensive than moving it while it's still a module boundary inside one codebase. Good first candidates are modules whose data no other module joins against, because their tables can move with them cleanly.

Incremental extraction is often called the **strangler fig pattern**: new functionality, and gradually more old functionality, is routed to a new service while the surrounding monolith keeps running, until the extracted piece fully replaces what the monolith did for that capability. It is a controlled, reversible migration instead of a risky big-bang rewrite.

examples.title: Decomposed by Verb vs. Decomposed by Capability
examples.code:
BY VERB (usually wrong):
  [create-order-service] [cancel-order-service] [ship-order-service]
  -- all three read/write the SAME "orders" table
  -- cancelling an order: client calls cancel-order-service, which
     must synchronously call create-order-service's internals (or a
     shared library) to check current status, then notify shipping

  Client request "cancel order 42":
    -> cancel-order-service
         -> (needs current status) --sync call--> create-order-service
         -> (needs to stop shipment) --sync call--> ship-order-service
    3 services, 2 extra network hops, for one logical action

BY CAPABILITY (better):
  [order-service]  -- owns order creation, cancellation, shipping
                       status, AND the orders table, as one unit

  Client request "cancel order 42":
    -> order-service handles the entire operation internally
       (in-process function calls, one transaction against one table)
    0 extra network hops for this logical action
examples.explanation: The verb-decomposed version turns one atomic client action into a chain of synchronous cross-service calls, each with its own latency, failure mode, and retry and timeout logic. All three services still share the same orders table, so the boundary gives no data-ownership benefit despite the deployment and operational overhead of three services. The capability-decomposed version keeps everything that reasons about an order's lifecycle in one service with one table, so "cancel an order" is a single in-process operation in a single transaction, and the service can change its internal logic (a new cancellation rule, a new status) without a synchronized change across three deployables.

examples.title: Decomposed by Table: The Distributed Join Problem
examples.code:
[users-service]  owns "users" table
[orders-service] owns "orders" table

Feature: "show a customer their order history with their name and
           current shipping address on each order"

Naive implementation:
  orders-service.get_orders(customer_id)
    -> for each order returned, synchronously call
       users-service.get_user(order.customer_id)
       to fetch name + address
  -- N orders means N extra network calls to users-service
     (an N+1 query problem, now happening ACROSS a network boundary
      instead of just across database tables)
examples.explanation: Splitting by table looked objective, since the schema already had two separate tables, but the feature needs both tables' data together. The boundary turns what would be a cheap SQL join inside one database into N network round trips to another service, one per order, which is slower and more fragile (each of the N calls can fail or time out on its own). Fixing it usually means denormalizing a copy of the needed user fields into orders-service's own data (kept in sync via events, accepting some staleness), or adding a batch endpoint (one call for all N customer IDs instead of N calls). The deeper lesson is that the table-based boundary was drawn without checking whether queries needed data from both sides of it.

examples.title: A Distributed Monolith Symptom: Forced Co-Deployment
examples.code:
payments-service v1.4 expects order-service to send:
  { "orderId": 42, "amountCents": 1999 }

order-service wants to change to:
  { "orderId": 42, "amount": { "cents": 1999, "currency": "USD" } }

Deploy sequence REQUIRED to avoid breaking production:
  1. Deploy payments-service v1.5, which accepts BOTH the old and
     new shapes (a compatibility shim)
  2. Deploy order-service's new version, which sends the new shape
  3. Later, deploy payments-service v1.6, which drops support for
     the old shape
  -- three coordinated deploys, in a specific order, across two
     "independent" services, for what was meant to be one change
examples.explanation: This is forced co-deployment in its clearest form. order-service and payments-service are nominally independent, but a routine change to the message format between them can't ship independently: it needs a carefully sequenced three-step rollout across both, to avoid a window where one side sends a shape the other can't parse. A well-drawn boundary would avoid the coupling (each side depends on a versioned, backward-compatible contract designed to allow additive changes), or would keep this logic in one service if the two always have to change together this tightly. Needing a three-deploy choreography for a routine field change is a symptom that the boundary isn't where the code's seams are. The sequence shown is the expand-and-contract pattern: it's the safe way to change a shared contract, and the cost of paying it for every routine change is what signals the problem.

misconceptions.description: The cleanest, most objective way to split a monolith into microservices is to give each database table its own service.
misconceptions.clarification: Splitting by table feels objective because the boundary already exists in the schema, but it draws the line by how data happens to be stored and not by which data is used together by features and queries. Most non-trivial features need data from more than one table, and a table-per-service boundary turns each of them into cross-service calls (often an N+1 pattern over the network) that would have been a cheap join inside one database. A better boundary groups tables that are used together into one service, based on business capability, and splits further only when a demonstrated need (independent scaling, independent team ownership) appears.

misconceptions.description: Having more microservices is inherently a sign of a more mature, more scalable architecture.
misconceptions.clarification: The number of services is not a proxy for architectural quality. A system split into many services along the wrong seams (by verb, by table, or just to have "microservices") commonly becomes a distributed monolith: all the network calls, deployment coordination, and operational overhead of a distributed system, while most services still have to change and deploy together, because the coupling never went away. It just moved from in-process function calls to network calls. A well-modularized monolith that hasn't needed to split yet is often healthier and easier to maintain than a prematurely over-decomposed set of tightly coupled services.

exercises.prompt: An e-commerce system decomposes 'placing an order' into four separate services: validate-cart-service, charge-payment-service, reserve-inventory-service, and send-confirmation-service, each called synchronously in sequence by the client (or a thin orchestrating layer) for every single checkout. Predict what happens to checkout latency and failure-handling complexity compared to a single order-service handling the whole flow, and explain why.
exercises.code:
Checkout flow, decomposed by verb, all synchronous:
  client -> validate-cart-service      (60ms)
         -> charge-payment-service      (300ms, calls an external payment processor)
         -> reserve-inventory-service   (80ms)
         -> send-confirmation-service   (50ms)
  Total: ~490ms IF every call succeeds on the first try, with NO retries

Each service is independently deployable and independently can fail,
timeout, or need a retry.
hints: Add up the latencies assuming everything succeeds -- but then ask what happens to that total if even ONE of the four calls needs a retry due to a transient failure.
Think about what has to happen if charge-payment-service succeeds but reserve-inventory-service then fails -- who is responsible for reversing the charge, and does that logic live in any one place?
Compare this to a single order-service handling validation, charging, reservation, and confirmation as one in-process, one-transaction operation.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Checkout latency becomes the sum of four sequential network calls (490ms best case) instead of one in-process operation, and each hop is an independent point of failure that needs its own timeout and retry handling, so worst-case latency with retries can go well past 490ms, and average latency is worse than an in-process call chain because round trips are added at every step. Failure handling gets much harder: if charge-payment-service succeeds but reserve-inventory-service then fails, something has to reverse the charge (a compensating action). Because the four services are separate deployables with no shared transaction, that reversal logic has to be built and maintained by hand, instead of relying on the all-or-nothing rollback of one database transaction in a single order-service.
exercises.solutionExplanation: This is the "one service per verb" anti-pattern in its clearest form: an operation that could be atomic inside one service is spread across four independently failing network calls. Latency accumulates additively across the chain, and every hop adds its own possible timeout, retry, and partial-failure case that has to be designed for. The worst case is the one where an earlier step (charging the card) succeeded and a later one (reserving inventory) failed, which needs a compensating transaction (refund or void the charge) that a single-service, single-transaction design would never need, since a failed database transaction would roll everything back. None of the four services can be deployed, scaled, or reasoned about independently for this flow, which is the distributed-monolith symptom: distribution's overhead without its benefits. Availability compounds the same way: if each of the four services is up 99.9% of the time, a checkout needing all four succeeds only about 99.6% of the time (0.999 to the fourth power), so the flow is less available than any one of its parts.

exercises.prompt: A team splits their application into users-service (owns the users table) and orders-service (owns the orders table). To display an order confirmation page (which needs the customer's name and shipping address alongside order details), orders-service synchronously calls users-service on every single order-detail page load. During a users-service outage, the orders-service's order-detail endpoint also goes down completely, even though nothing about orders themselves is broken. Diagnose the architectural problem and propose a fix.
exercises.code:
def get_order_detail(order_id):
    order = orders_db.query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = %s", order_id)
    # synchronous cross-service call on every single request, no fallback
    customer = users_service_client.get_user(order.customer_id)
    return {
        "order": order,
        "customerName": customer.name,
        "shippingAddress": customer.address,
    }

# during a users-service outage: users_service_client.get_user() times out
# or errors -> get_order_detail() raises -> order-detail page is DOWN,
# even though orders_db and all order data are completely fine
hints: This is the table-based decomposition problem from the explanation: orders-service needs data that lives in users-service's table for a routine, high-traffic page. Does that dependency show up anywhere except at request time?
Right now, orders-service's availability for this endpoint is capped by users-service's availability, even though the underlying data (order details) is completely healthy. What would decouple that?

Consider what it would look like to keep a copy of just the fields orders-service actually needs (name, shipping address at order time), updated asynchronously, rather than fetching them live on every single page view.
exercises.solutionCode:
# FIX: denormalize the specific fields orders-service actually needs,
# captured AT ORDER TIME (which is also more correct -- an order's
# confirmation should show the shipping address as it was when the
# order was placed, not the customer's CURRENT address if they've since moved)

def place_order(customer_id, items):
    customer = users_service_client.get_user(customer_id)  # called ONCE, at order time
    order = orders_db.insert(
        customer_id=customer_id,
        items=items,
        customer_name_snapshot=customer.name,
        shipping_address_snapshot=customer.address,
    )
    return order

def get_order_detail(order_id):
    order = orders_db.query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = %s", order_id)
    return {
        "order": order,
        "customerName": order.customer_name_snapshot,
        "shippingAddress": order.shipping_address_snapshot,
    }
    # no cross-service call at all on this hot, high-traffic read path --
    # orders-service's availability for this page no longer depends on
    # users-service's availability
exercises.solutionExplanation: The root problem is a table-based service boundary combined with a synchronous cross-service call on a hot read path. orders-service's most common, highest-traffic operation (viewing an order) depends on users-service being up, even though the operation isn't about users-service's responsibilities: it needs two fields. Any query needing both tables pays an availability cost (and an N+1-style latency cost at higher volume) that a differently drawn boundary wouldn't. The fix denormalizes the needed fields into orders-service's own data, captured once at order-placement time, which is also more correct: an order confirmation should show the shipping address as it was when the order was placed, not wherever the customer lives now. That removes the synchronous dependency from the hot path, so users-service can be fully down and order-detail pages keep working, because orders-service owns everything it needs for that page.

assessments.prompt: A team notices that two of their 'independent' microservices almost always need to be deployed together, in a specific order, whenever the message format between them changes. What does this symptom most directly indicate?
options: This is normal and expected behavior for any two microservices that communicate with each other.
The two services are not actually independently deployable in practice.
The two services are using the wrong network protocol between them and should switch from REST to gRPC.
The services need a faster network connection between them to reduce deployment coordination time.
assessments.explanation: Forced, ordered co-deployment is one of the clearest symptoms of a distributed-monolith boundary: if two services can't change independently, the boundary isn't providing the independence microservices are supposed to buy, however the code is organized into deployables. The “The two services are using the wrong…” option misdiagnoses it as a protocol choice: switching REST to gRPC wouldn't fix a coupling problem in contract compatibility and ownership. The “This is normal and expected behavior…” option is wrong: well-bounded services with stable or properly versioned contracts shouldn't need ordered deploys for routine changes, so that need is the symptom and not the baseline. The “The services need a faster network connection…” option mistakes a coupling problem for a network-speed problem: a faster network does nothing to remove the need for coordinated deploys.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a team about to split their monolith into microservices why 'one service per table' and 'one service per verb' are both commonly-reached-for but usually wrong ways to draw the boundaries, and what a better approach looks like.
assessments.modelAnswer: Both heuristics are attractive because they feel objective and mechanical: you can look at a schema or a list of API operations and draw lines without a judgment call about the business domain. That is also their weakness. They optimize for something easy to see (an existing table, an existing verb) instead of how the system's data and logic are used together. "One service per table" mirrors the schema, but nearly every feature needs data from more than one table (an order confirmation needs the customer's name and address alongside order details, a product listing needs inventory alongside pricing), so everyday operations have to reach across a service boundary. A cheap SQL join becomes slow, fragile cross-service calls, and one service's basic read path comes to depend on another service's availability. "One service per verb" mirrors the list of operations, splitting "create an order," "cancel an order," and "ship an order" into separate services, but cancelling an order needs to check status, adjust inventory, and possibly issue a refund, which now requires synchronous coordination across several services for what should be one atomic action. A better approach draws boundaries around cohesive business capabilities: a piece of the domain that changes for its own reasons, that one team can own end to end, and that owns its data so nothing else reaches into its storage. In practice that means starting from a well-modularized monolith whose internal boundaries track business capabilities, and extracting a module into its own service only when there's a demonstrated reason (a scaling need, a team that needs its own deployment cadence, a distinct technology requirement), instead of deciding every boundary upfront from the schema or the API surface before anyone has lived with the system long enough to know where its seams are.

assessments.prompt: A billing service and a support-ticketing service each have their own internal notion of a 'customer,' with different fields and different invariants for each. Is this a sign of duplicated, sloppy modeling that should be unified into one shared customer definition?
options: Yes, but only because billing and support-ticketing are both customer-facing features and should therefore share a database table.
Yes -- there should always be exactly one canonical definition of any business term shared across every service in the system.
No, but only because billing services are legally required to maintain a separate customer definition from support systems.

No -- this is an example of a bounded context: a boundary drawn around a part of the domain where terms mean one specific thing internally, and a neighboring service using a similar-sounding term differently is expected and fine, not a modeling mistake.
assessments.explanation: A customer in the billing service can carry different fields and invariants than a customer in support ticketing, and that's fine: they're different bounded contexts, not the same concept duplicated sloppily. The “Yes -- there should always be exactly…” option insists on one canonical definition everywhere, which contradicts the idea. The “Yes, but only because billing and support-ticketing…” option invents a database-sharing requirement, and would reintroduce the shared-table problem. The “No, but only because billing services…” option fabricates a legal requirement that has nothing to do with bounded contexts.

assessments.prompt: What makes a 'distributed monolith' worse than either a well-factored monolith or a well-factored set of microservices?
options: It carries the full operational overhead of a distributed system (network calls, independent deployments to coordinate, separate logging to correlate, retries and timeouts) while still keeping the monolith's actual coupling problem, since the pieces can't really change or deploy independently -- paying distribution's complexity tax without collecting its benefits.
It is only a problem when the number of services exceeds fifty.
It has fewer total lines of code than either alternative, making it harder to find bugs.
It always runs on more expensive cloud infrastructure than either alternative.
assessments.explanation: A distributed monolith has the operational overhead of microservices while keeping the monolith's coupling, because the pieces can't really change or deploy independently, so you pay the complexity tax of distribution without collecting its benefits. The “It has fewer total lines of code…” option invents an unrelated code-volume claim. The “It always runs on more expensive cloud…” option fabricates a cost claim. The “It is only a problem…” option invents an arbitrary service-count threshold: the symptoms show up with as few as two or three services.

assessments.prompt: When should a module be extracted out of a well-modularized monolith into its own separately deployed service?
options: Whenever the monolith's total codebase exceeds an arbitrary line-of-code threshold.
As soon as the monolith is created, so that the system is 'microservices-native' from day one.
Only once there's a concrete, demonstrated reason.
Never -- the concept argues that services should always remain part of a single monolith regardless of team or scaling needs.
assessments.explanation: Modules should be split out only once there's a demonstrated reason: a scaling need for just that piece, a team that needs to deploy independently, or a technology requirement. Splitting too early, before the domain boundaries are understood from living with the monolith, tends to reproduce the wrong-boundary symptoms. The “As soon as the monolith is created…” option contradicts the advice to start with a monolith. The “Whenever the monolith's total codebase exceeds…” option invents an arbitrary line-count threshold. The “Never -- the concept argues that services…” option overstates the position: extraction is appropriate once a real reason exists.

concepts.title: API Gateways
concepts.description: Once you have more than a handful of backend services, clients shouldn't need to know about any of them individually -- an API gateway gives them one front door, and centralizes the cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate limiting, routing) that would otherwise be duplicated in every service.
learningObjectives: Explain the core problem an API gateway solves for clients calling many backend services.
List the cross-cutting concerns a gateway typically centralizes: routing, authentication, rate limiting, and request/response translation.
Explain why the gateway itself becomes a critical path requiring the same high-availability treatment as any other load-balanced, stateless service.
Distinguish an API gateway (edge, client-facing) from a service mesh (internal, service-to-service) and explain why they solve different problems.
Identify the anti-pattern of putting business logic in the gateway and explain why that undermines the boundary work done elsewhere.

sections.heading: One Front Door for Many Backends
sections.body:
Once a system is decomposed into multiple services, however well the boundaries were drawn, a client (a mobile app, a browser, a third-party integrator) faces a problem: which of these N services does it call for a given feature, and does it now have to implement authentication, retry logic, and rate-limit handling separately against every one of them? An **API gateway** sits between clients and the backend services, presents one entry point, and routes each incoming request to whichever backend handles it.

This isn't only a convenience for the client. It moves a whole category of concerns that would otherwise have to be implemented correctly inside *every* backend service into one place. Without a gateway, each of your N services needs its own authentication logic, its own rate limiting, its own TLS termination, and its own exposure to the outside world. With a gateway, backend services can often be unreachable from outside the internal network and only need to trust that a request reaching them already passed the gateway's checks.

sections.heading: What a Gateway Does
sections.body:
**Routing** is the most basic function: mapping an incoming request's path, host, or headers to the right backend service (`/api/orders/*` goes to order-service, `/api/users/*` to users-service). It's also the natural place to translate between protocols, such as accepting REST/JSON from the public internet and calling internal gRPC services, the translation-layer role from the REST vs. gRPC lesson.

**Authentication and authorization** are commonly centralized at the gateway: validate the caller's token or API key once at the edge instead of re-implementing validation in every backend, and reject clearly unauthorized requests before they consume a backend's resources. **Rate limiting and quota enforcement** also belong at the edge: since the gateway sees every request regardless of destination, it's the one place that can enforce a per-client or per-API-key limit across the *whole* API surface, not just one service's slice of it. Beyond these three, gateways commonly handle TLS termination, request/response transformation (reshaping a legacy backend's response into the shape the public API promises), and centralized logging and metrics for every request entering the system.

sections.heading: The Cost: A New Critical Path and a New Coordination Point
sections.body:
A gateway that sits in front of every request is by definition a critical path for the whole system. If it's down, every backend behind it is unreachable from outside, however healthy those backends are. So the gateway needs the high-availability treatment from the load balancing and statelessness lesson: it must be scaled horizontally behind its own load balancer, and it must be stateless (or keep whatever state it needs, like rate-limit counters, in a shared store) so any instance can handle any request. It also adds a network hop to every request, usually small next to backend time but counted in your latency budget. A single gateway instance is as much a single point of failure as a single backend instance, and being "just infrastructure" doesn't exempt it.

There's an organizational cost too. A gateway's routing and policy configuration becomes a shared resource that potentially every team's changes pass through, which can turn it into a coordination bottleneck: a team that wants to add a backend service or change a rate-limit tier depends on however the gateway's configuration is owned and reviewed. That doesn't go away by being ignored. It needs an ownership model (self-service configuration with guardrails is a common answer), or it recreates at the infrastructure layer the forced-coordination problem the service-boundaries lesson called a smell.

sections.heading: Gateway vs. Service Mesh: Two Different Traffic Directions
sections.body:
It's easy to conflate an API gateway with a **service mesh**, but they handle traffic moving in different directions. The gateway handles **north-south traffic**: requests entering the system from outside (clients, third parties) heading toward internal services. A service mesh (tools like Istio or Linkerd, typically implemented as sidecar proxies deployed next to each service) handles **east-west traffic**: service-to-service calls inside the system, providing automatic retries, mutual TLS between internal services, and fine-grained internal routing (canary releases, circuit breaking) for calls that never touch an external client.

A mature system commonly runs both, for different reasons: the gateway answers "how does the outside world reach us," and the mesh answers "how do our own fifteen services reach each other reliably." Expecting one to do the other's job, for example by routing all internal service-to-service traffic back out through the edge gateway, adds latency and turns an internal implementation detail into edge-gateway configuration churn.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake: Putting Business Logic in the Gateway
sections.body: Because the gateway is a central place to add "just one more thing," it's tempting to put business logic there: pricing calculations, feature-flag behavior specific to one backend's domain, response shaping that encodes domain rules instead of format translation. This is a mistake for the reason the service-boundaries lesson gave: business logic belongs inside the service that owns the business capability, not in shared, cross-cutting infrastructure that every team's traffic passes through. Once domain logic lives in the gateway, changing it means touching a shared resource that is supposed to stay generic and stable, and two backend teams who need slightly different behavior for their own domains must negotiate over one central config instead of changing their own service. The gateway should stay thin (routing, authentication, rate limiting, protocol translation, observability) and leave anything domain-specific to the services that own that domain.

examples.title: Without a Gateway vs. With One
examples.code:
WITHOUT a gateway -- client must know about every backend directly:
  [Mobile App] --auth+call--> order-service   (implements its own auth check)
              --auth+call--> users-service    (implements its own auth check)
              --auth+call--> inventory-service (implements its own auth check)
  -- 3 services, each independently exposed to the internet
  -- 3 separate auth implementations that must all be correct and consistent
  -- app needs to know 3 different hostnames/ports and keep them all in sync

WITH a gateway -- one front door:
  [Mobile App] --auth+call--> [API Gateway] --routes to--> order-service
                                             --routes to--> users-service
                                             --routes to--> inventory-service
  -- app only knows ONE hostname; auth is checked ONCE, at the gateway
  -- order/users/inventory-service can be entirely unreachable from
     the public internet, trusting requests that already reached them
examples.explanation: The without-gateway version multiplies every cross-cutting concern (auth, TLS, rate limiting, internet exposure) by the number of backends. That means N implementations that must all be correct and stay consistent as requirements change, and a missed update to one service's auth logic is a security gap that's easy to introduce unnoticed. The with-gateway version centralizes each concern in one place, checked once per request however many backends sit behind it, and lets every backend be deployed without direct internet exposure, which reduces the attack surface and the amount of security-critical code that has to be right independently in each service.

examples.title: Gateway Routing and Rate Limiting Configuration
examples.code:
routes:
  - pathPrefix: /api/orders
    backend: order-service
    protocol: grpc          # gateway translates REST/JSON in -> gRPC out
  - pathPrefix: /api/users
    backend: users-service
    protocol: http

rateLimits:
  - apiKeyTier: free
    limit: 100 requests / minute, ACROSS ALL routes combined
  - apiKeyTier: paid
    limit: 5000 requests / minute, ACROSS ALL routes combined

auth:
  requireValidToken: true   # applies to EVERY route above, enforced once
  onInvalidToken: reject with 401, never forward to backend
examples.explanation: This configuration shows the gateway doing the three core jobs in one place. Routing maps path prefixes to backends, including a protocol translation from public REST/JSON to an internal gRPC service. Rate limiting is enforced per API key across the client's *entire* usage of the API, which no single backend could enforce because each one sees only its slice of that client's traffic. Authentication is checked once, and invalid requests are rejected before reaching a backend, so order-service and users-service never handle an unauthenticated request. The tier limits apply across all routes combined, a global view that is only possible because the gateway sees every request regardless of destination.

examples.title: The Business-Logic-in-the-Gateway Anti-Pattern
examples.explanation: The bad version puts a business decision, how much discount a premium customer gets, into the gateway, which is supposed to be shared, generic infrastructure that every team's traffic passes through. When a second service needs its own, possibly different, discount rule, the only place for it is also the shared gateway config, which starts to collect every backend team's domain rules in one tangled, centrally owned place. The better version keeps the gateway to routing, with no domain decisions, and lets order-service own its pricing logic, as the service-boundaries lesson would recommend for any business capability. If a second service needs different pricing rules, it implements its own with no coordination through the gateway.

misconceptions.description: An API gateway is basically just a fancy name for a reverse proxy or load balancer sitting in front of your services.
misconceptions.clarification: A reverse proxy or load balancer routes and distributes traffic across backend instances, and a gateway does that as part of its routing function. But a gateway typically adds a layer of cross-cutting policy on top: authentication and authorization, per-client rate limiting and quotas across the whole API surface, request/response transformation and protocol translation, and API-level observability. A plain load balancer has no concept of an API key's tier or of JSON-to-gRPC translation. A gateway is a load balancer plus a policy and translation layer built for API traffic.

misconceptions.description: Once authentication and rate limiting are handled at the gateway, individual backend services don't need to think about security at all.
misconceptions.clarification: Centralizing auth and rate limiting at the edge is valuable, but treating it as the only line of defense creates a single point of security failure. If the gateway is misconfigured, bypassed (a service reachable directly, not only through the gateway, because of a network misconfiguration), or has a bug in its enforcement logic, backend services with no security checks of their own have no fallback. Defense in depth still matters: backends should still validate that a request carries the identity and authorization context the gateway is supposed to have attached, instead of trusting that every request they receive passed every gateway check.

exercises.prompt: A company runs a single API gateway instance (no load balancer, no additional replicas) in front of 12 healthy, horizontally-scaled backend services. Predict what happens to the overall system's availability if that one gateway instance crashes, even though all 12 backend services remain fully healthy and reachable on the internal network. Then predict what changes if the gateway itself is deployed as a stateless pool of instances behind its own load balancer.
exercises.code:
CURRENT setup:
  [Clients] -> [1x API Gateway instance] -> 12x healthy backend services
  (gateway has no replicas, no load balancer in front of it)

ALTERNATIVE setup:
  [Clients] -> [Load Balancer] -> [Nx API Gateway instances] -> 12x backend services
hints: Every external request has to pass through the gateway to reach ANY backend. If the one gateway instance is down, can clients reach backend service 1 through 12 at all?

This is the exact same single-point-of-failure argument made about a single vertically-scaled machine in the scaling fundamentals module -- does being 'just infrastructure' rather than a backend service change that argument?
In the alternative setup, what has to be true about each gateway instance (statelessness) for the load balancer to route to any of them interchangeably?
exercises.expectedAnswer: In the current setup, the whole system becomes unreachable from outside the moment the single gateway instance crashes, however healthy the 12 backends are. The gateway is a single point of failure in front of everything, and being "just routing infrastructure" doesn't exempt it from the single-machine failure argument. In the alternative setup, losing one of N gateway instances reduces total gateway capacity by roughly 1/N (assuming the load balancer's health checks detect the failed instance and route around it), and the system stays reachable as long as one gateway instance is healthy. That requires each gateway instance to be stateless (rate-limit counters and any session-like data kept in a shared store) so any instance can correctly handle any request.
exercises.solutionExplanation: A single gateway instance is as much a single point of failure as a single backend server. All 12 backends can be perfectly healthy, and it doesn't matter if nothing outside the network can reach the gateway, because the gateway is on the only path in. This reuses the vertical-vs-horizontal scaling argument from the scaling fundamentals module: a gateway's importance (it fronts everything) makes its availability more critical, not less, so exempting it from horizontal scaling and load balancing because it's "infrastructure" gets it backwards. Making the gateway stateless and running a load-balanced pool applies the same fix as any other horizontally scaled tier: any healthy instance can handle any request, so losing one degrades capacity proportionally instead of cutting off the whole backend fleet.

exercises.prompt: A platform team owns the shared API gateway. Over time, individual backend teams have each added their own domain-specific request-transformation rules directly into the gateway's central configuration (e.g., order-service's team added order-total rounding logic; inventory-service's team added stock-threshold business rules). Now, every team's change to their own domain logic requires a review and deploy from the platform team, creating a growing backlog and slowing every team down. Diagnose the architectural mistake and propose a fix.
exercises.code:
gateway_config.yaml (owned and reviewed by the platform team):
  routes:
    - path: /api/orders/*
      backend: order-service
      transform: round_order_total_to_nearest_cent   # order-service's rule
    - path: /api/inventory/*
      backend: inventory-service
      transform: apply_low_stock_threshold_flag        # inventory-service's rule
  # every one of these transform rules requires the PLATFORM team to
  # review and deploy, even though the LOGIC belongs to other teams
hints: Whose business capability does 'rounding an order total' or 'flagging low stock' actually belong to -- the platform team's, or order-service's and inventory-service's respectively?
This is the same anti-pattern named directly in the explanation -- business logic living in shared, centrally-owned infrastructure rather than in the service that owns the corresponding domain.
What would it look like for order-service and inventory-service to each own and deploy their own transformation logic independently, with the gateway doing only routing?
exercises.solutionCode:
# FIX: move each team's domain logic OUT of the gateway and into their
# own service, where they can change and deploy it independently

# gateway_config.yaml -- now genuinely thin, only routing:
  routes:
    - path: /api/orders/*
      backend: order-service      # no transform rule here anymore
    - path: /api/inventory/*
      backend: inventory-service  # no transform rule here anymore

# inside order-service (owned and deployed independently by its own team):
  def get_order_response(order):
      order.total = round_to_nearest_cent(order.total)   # lives HERE now
      return order

# inside inventory-service (owned and deployed independently by its own team):
  def get_inventory_response(item):
      item.lowStockFlag = item.quantity < LOW_STOCK_THRESHOLD  # lives HERE
      return item
exercises.solutionExplanation: The mistake is business logic in the gateway: order-total rounding and low-stock flagging are domain rules that belong to order-service and inventory-service, but they ended up in the gateway, shared infrastructure that should stay generic, because it was a convenient place to add "just one transformation." The consequence is the coordination bottleneck described earlier: every domain team's routine change to its own business rules now goes through the platform team's review and deploy cycle, turning an independent, fast change into a shared queue. The fix moves each rule back into the service that owns the capability, so each team can change and deploy its own logic independently, and leaves the gateway doing only routing, with no domain decisions in shared configuration that every team has to get one owner to change. If the platform team still needs to offer shared transformations, give teams a plugin mechanism they own and deploy themselves, so the gateway stays generic.

assessments.prompt: A team wants to enforce a rate limit of 1,000 requests per minute per API key, applied across a client's combined usage of order-service, users-service, and inventory-service (not 1,000 per service separately). Where does this rate limit logic best belong, and why?
options: It cannot be enforced accurately in a distributed system and should be approximated by tripling each service's individual limit, which gives roughly the same result because clients tend to spread their requests evenly over the three services.

At the API gateway, since it is the only component that sees every request from a given API key across all three backend services, making it the only place that can enforce a limit on the client's combined, cross-service usage.
Inside a shared code library that each of the three services imports and calls independently.
Inside each of the three backend services independently, since each service should be responsible for protecting itself.
assessments.explanation: A combined, cross-service limit requires visibility into a client's total usage across all three services, and only the gateway, which sits in front of every request regardless of destination, has it. Each backend service alone sees only its slice of that client's traffic and can't know how many requests the client just sent to the other two. The “Inside each of the three backend services…” option can only enforce a per-service limit, not the combined one, however well each service implements it. The “Inside a shared code library that each…” option has the same problem: even with shared code, each instance observes only its own traffic unless the library talks to a shared central counter, which reinvents part of what the gateway already does. The “It cannot be enforced accurately…” option is a rough approximation that overshoots or undershoots depending on how traffic splits across the three services, not a real solution.

assessments.prompt: A colleague asks: "Our API gateway is just a routing layer. Why does it need its own load balancer and multiple replicas like a backend service?" Explain why the gateway needs the same high-availability treatment as any other service, referring to the earlier scaling and load-balancing lessons.
assessments.modelAnswer: The question treats "just a routing layer" as if that makes the gateway less critical, when it makes it more critical. Every request from every client, headed to any backend service, passes through the gateway first, so the gateway's availability is a hard ceiling on the availability of everything behind it. This is the single-point-of-failure argument from the vertical-vs-horizontal scaling lesson, applied to infrastructure instead of a backend service: a single gateway instance, however well it performs while healthy, is one machine that can crash, need a restart for a deploy, or hit a resource limit, and when it does all twelve perfectly healthy backend services become unreachable from outside because there's no other way in. Being "just routing" doesn't exempt a component from being a single point of failure; sitting on the only path into the system gives its failure a larger blast radius than almost any individual backend's. The fix is the one from the load-balancing and statelessness lesson: run multiple gateway instances behind a load balancer, and make each instance stateless, so anything it tracks across requests, such as per-API-key rate-limit counters, lives in a shared external store and not in one instance's memory. Then the load balancer can route any request to any healthy instance, and losing one instance reduces gateway capacity by roughly one over the number of instances instead of cutting off access to the whole system. The gateway has a stronger case for these availability requirements than other services, because everything else depends on it being reachable.

assessments.prompt: A team wants automatic retries, mutual TLS, and fine-grained canary routing for calls between their own internal services, none of which ever touch an external client. Which tool is the better fit, a gateway or a service mesh, and why?
options: A service mesh, since it handles east-west traffic -- service-to-service calls entirely inside the system -- providing exactly these capabilities, whereas the gateway's job is north-south traffic entering the system from outside.

Neither -- these capabilities can only be achieved by routing all internal traffic back out through the edge API gateway, where the gateway can apply mutual TLS and retries to each call before sending it back inside the private network again.
An API gateway, since only gateways can perform mutual TLS between two internal services.
An API gateway, since gateways and service meshes are two names for the exact same tool applied to different traffic.
assessments.explanation: A service mesh handles east-west traffic, service-to-service calls inside the system, and provides automatic retries, mutual TLS between internal services, and fine-grained internal routing such as canary releases and circuit breaking. The gateway handles north-south traffic entering the system from outside. The “An API gateway, since gateways and service…” option contradicts that distinction by treating the two as one tool. The “Neither -- these capabilities can only…” option describes the mistake of routing internal traffic back out through the edge gateway, which adds latency and turns an internal detail into edge-gateway configuration churn. The “An API gateway, since only gateways can…” option fabricates a restriction: mutual TLS isn't exclusive to gateways.

assessments.prompt: A team centralizes authentication and rate limiting entirely at the API gateway and removes all security checks from their backend services, reasoning the gateway already handles it. What risk does this leave open?
options: This is only a risk for services using gRPC, not for services using REST.
The only risk is a minor performance slowdown, since the gateway would simply run the same checks twice.

If the gateway is ever misconfigured, bypassed (a backend reachable directly due to a network misconfiguration), or has a bug in its enforcement logic, backend services with zero security checks of their own have no fallback protection at all -- defense in depth still matters.
No risk at all -- the concept states that backend services never need any security logic once a gateway is in place.
assessments.explanation: Relying on the gateway as the only line of defense creates a single point of security failure. If it's misconfigured, bypassed, or has a bug in its enforcement logic, backends should still validate that a request carries the identity and authorization context the gateway is supposed to have attached, instead of trusting every request. The “No risk at all -- the concept…” option contradicts the warning against exactly this assumption. The “The only risk is a minor performance…” option turns a security gap into a performance concern, which isn't the risk. The “This is only a risk for services…” option invents a protocol-specific restriction.

assessments.prompt: What goes wrong when a mobile app calls three backend services directly, each implementing its own authentication check, instead of going through a gateway?
options: Each backend service becomes automatically stateful as a result of implementing its own authentication.
Nothing goes wrong functionally -- it is described as a purely stylistic difference with no real consequence.
The mobile app becomes physically incapable of making more than one request per session without a gateway present.

There are now three separate auth implementations that all must be correct and kept consistent as requirements change, three services independently exposed to the internet, and the app must track three different hostnames/ports -- multiplying a cross-cutting concern by the number of backends instead of centralizing it.
assessments.explanation: Without a gateway there are three separate auth implementations that must all be correct and consistent, three services independently exposed to the internet, and an app that has to know three hostnames and keep them in sync. The cross-cutting concern is multiplied instead of centralized. The “Nothing goes wrong functionally…” option dismisses a real cost: a missed auth update becomes a security gap that's easy to introduce unnoticed. The “The mobile app becomes physically incapable…” option invents a limit on request counts. The “Each backend service becomes automatically stateful…” option is a non sequitur: implementing authentication has no bearing on a service's statelessness.
